papers.title_in_file: A Survey of Quantum Learning Theory
papers.version_note: arXiv:1701.06806v2 [quant-ph], 24 Apr 2017; the text is the paper the record names.
papers.what_it_is: A survey of quantum learning theory (exact learning from membership queries, PAC and agnostic learning from classical or quantum examples), sketching proofs of results from other work and the authors' own earlier paper.

quotes: The number of quantum membership queries needed to exactly learn a target concept can be polynomially smaller than the number of classical membership queries, but not much smaller than that.
Can we ﬁnd practical machine learning problems with a large provable quantum speed-up?

existing.note: Both halves of the stored value are in Section 6; the second half is given here as a second quote.
quotes: For the distribution-independent models of PAC and agnostic learning, quantum examples give no signiﬁcant advantage over classical random examples
In contrast, for some ﬁxed distributions (e.g., uniform) quantum examples can be much better than classical examples.

existing.note: Section 6 states the claim without a condition, but the later sections give it only under complexity-theoretic assumptions: Theorem 5.1 needs that no efficient classical algorithm factors Blum integers, and Theorem 5.2 needs that classical one-way functions exist. The introduction also says 'under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions'.
existing.value: The survey states that there exist concept classes that can be learned superpolynomially faster by quantum computers than by classical computers, for instance based on Shor's or Simon's algorithm; its later sections give these separations conditional on a complexity-theoretic assumption, namely that no efficient classical algorithm factors Blum integers or that classical one-way functions exist.

assertions.value: The authors state that the survey describes the main known results for three models of learning: exact learning from membership queries, and Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) and agnostic learning from classical or quantum examples.

assertions.value: The authors state that the survey focuses on the theoretical side of quantum machine learning, which they call quantum learning theory, and describes the main results in three learning models with sketched proofs.
quotes: in this survey we focus on the theoretical side of quantum machine learning: quantum learning theory.
We will describe (and sketch proofs of) the main results that have been obtained in three main learning models.

assertions.value: The authors state that some of the recent work applying quantum algorithms to specific machine learning problems is heuristic in nature rather than mathematically rigorous, and that some approaches suggest exponential speed-ups but depend on assumptions that in some cases also make efficient classical machine learning possible.

assertions.value: The authors state in their preview that if the complexity measure is only the number of queries, quantum exact learners can be polynomially more efficient than classical ones but not more, and that if the measure is time, then under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions some concept classes can be learned much faster from quantum membership queries.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the usual distribution-independent PAC model quantum and classical sample complexity are equal up to constant factors for every concept class, and that when time is the measure, under reasonable complexity-theoretic assumptions, some concept classes can be PAC learned much faster by quantum learners even from classical examples.
quotes: in the usual distribution-independent PAC model, quantum and classical sample complexity are equal up to constant factors, for every concept class C.

assertions.value: The authors report that the proof sketch invokes results of Anthony and Bartlett and of Bartlett and Long on the γ-fat-shattering dimension, and that Aaronson uses bounds on quantum random access codes to show d = O(n/γ2) (gamma squared, printed flat).

assertions.value: The authors report that Cheng et al. studied how many states are sufficient to learn an unknown quantum measurement, finding the answer linear in the dimension of the space and so exponential in the number of qubits.
quotes: Here the answer turns out to be linear in the dimension of the space, so exponential in the number of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that in many ways the best measure of efficient learning is low time complexity, because low sample complexity is necessary but not sufficient when finding a good hypothesis still takes much time.
quotes: In many ways, the best measure of eﬃcient learning is low time complexity.
the information-theoretic suﬃciency of a small sample is not much help in practice if ﬁnding a good hypothesis still takes much time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' view, without evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is widely assumed that classical computers cannot efficiently factor Blum integers, and that Kearns and Valiant had already constructed a factoring-based concept class with small VC dimension that is not efficiently learnable classically.
quotes: It is widely assumed that classical computers cannot eﬃciently factor Blum integers
that is not eﬃciently learnable.

assertions.value: The authors state (Servedio and Gortler) that if there is no efficient classical algorithm for factoring Blum integers, then there exists a concept class efficiently PAC learnable by quantum computers but not by classical computers, and there exists one efficiently exactly learnable from membership queries by quantum computers but not by classical computers.
quotes: If there is no eﬃcient classical algorithm for factoring Blum integers, then
there exists a concept class that is eﬃciently PAC learnable by quantum computers but not by classical computers;
there exists a concept class that is eﬃciently exactly learnable from membership queries by quantum computers but not by classical computers.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem attributed to other work; it is conditional on a factoring assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state (Servedio and Gortler) that if classical one-way functions exist, then there is a concept class that is efficiently exactly learnable from membership queries by quantum computers but not by classical computers, irrespective of whether the one-way function can be broken by a quantum computer.
quotes: If classical one-way functions exist, then there is a concept class C that is eﬃciently exactly learnable from membership queries by quantum computers but not by classical computers.
irrespective of whether that one-way function can be broken by a quantum computer!
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem attributed to other work; it is conditional on a one-way-function assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state that for learning DNF under the uniform distribution from classical examples the best upper bound is quasi-polynomial time, that with membership queries DNF is known to be learnable in polynomial time under the uniform distribution, and that polynomial-time learnability without membership queries is a longstanding open problem.

DNF formulas are known to be learnable in polynomial time under uniform D [Jac97]
polynomial-time learnability without membership queries is a longstanding open problem.

assertions.value: The authors state that if the target is an s-term DNF then there exists an n-bit parity function that agrees with c on a 1/2+Ω(1/s) fraction of the inputs, and that the Goldreich-Levin algorithm with membership queries can find such a parity function, giving a weak learner.

the Goldreich-Levin algorithm [GL89] can be used to eﬃciently ﬁnd such a parity function with the help of membership queries.

assertions.value: The authors state that the key to the quantum DNF learner is to replace Goldreich-Levin by Fourier sampling from uniform quantum examples; since a parity with correlation Ω(1/s) with the target is output with probability Ω(1/s2) (s squared, printed flat), poly(s) runs give a weak hypothesis, and membership queries are no longer required.
quotes: The key to the quantum learner is to observe that one can replace Goldreich-Levin by Fourier sampling from uniform quantum examples
Fourier sampling outputs that S with probability Ω(1/s2).
we do not require the use of membership queries anymore.

assertions.value: The authors state (Bshouty and Jackson) that the concept class of s-term DNF is efficiently PAC learnable under the uniform distribution from quantum examples.
quotes: The concept class of s-term DNF is eﬃciently PAC learnable under the uniform distribution from quantum examples.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a linear function f(x) = a · x mod 2, Fourier sampling recovers a perfectly with O(1) quantum sample complexity and O(n) time complexity, whereas classical learners need Ω(n) examples because each classical example gives at most one bit of information.

we can perfectly recover a with O(1) quantum sample complexity and O(n) time complexity.
classical learners need Ω(n) examples to learn f

assertions.value: The authors state that a trivial classical learner for k-juntas has time complexity O(nk) and the best known upper bound [MOS04] is O(nkω/(ω+1)) with ω ∈ [2, 2.38], and that learning k-juntas time-efficiently for k = O(log n) is a notorious bottleneck in classical learning theory, being a special case of DNF learning.

is a notorious bottleneck in classical learning theory, since it is a special case of DNF learning

assertions.value: The authors state that Bshouty and Jackson's DNF learner implies that k-juntas can be learned from uniform quantum examples using poly(2k, n) quantum examples and time for fixed ε, δ.

assertions.value: The authors state (Atici and Servedio) that there is a quantum algorithm for learning k-juntas under the uniform distribution that uses O(k log(k)/ε) uniform quantum examples, a number of uniform classical examples exponential in k (O(2k) in the text layer), and time O(nk log(k)/ε + 2k log(1/ε)).
quotes: There exists a quantum algorithm for learning k-juntas under the uniform distribution that uses O(k log(k)/ε) uniform quantum examples, O(2k) uniform classical examples, and O(nk log(k)/ε + 2k log(1/ε)) time.
assertions.certainty_reason: A theorem attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors report that the idea of the proof is to use Fourier sampling from quantum examples to find the junta variables with non-negligible influence, and then to use uniform classical examples to learn almost all of the truth-table of the function on those variables.

to learn (almost all of) the truth-table of the function on those variables.

assertions.value: The authors report that Belovs gives a tight analysis of the number of quantum membership queries needed to exactly learn k-juntas whose underlying k-bit function is symmetric: for OR or Majority, O(k1/4) quantum membership queries suffice (k to the power 1/4, printed flat), while for Majority Θ(k) classical membership queries are required, a fourth-power separation.

For the case of Majority, Θ(k) classical membership queries are required, giving a fourth-power separation

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the number of quantum membership queries needed to exactly learn a target concept can be polynomially smaller than the number of classical membership queries, but not much smaller than that.

assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion summarizing results the survey cites from other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that for every concept class the classical and quantum sample complexities are the same up to constant factors in the distribution-independent PAC and agnostic models, while for some fixed distributions such as the uniform one quantum examples can be much better than classical examples.
quotes: for every concept class, the classical and quantum sample complexities are the same up to constant factors.
In contrast, for some ﬁxed distributions (e.g., uniform) quantum examples can be much better than classical examples.
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion summarizing results the survey cites from other work.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that there exist concept classes that can be learned superpolynomially faster by quantum computers than by classical computers, for instance based on Shor's or Simon's algorithm, in both the model of exact learning with membership queries and the PAC model, and that with uniform quantum examples DNF and juntas can be learned much more efficiently than is known classically.
quotes: There exist concept classes that can be learned superpolynomially faster by quantum computers than by classical computers, for instance based on Shor’s or Simon’s algorithm.
This holds both in the model of exact learning with membership queries, and in the model of PAC-learning.
DNF and juntas can be learned much more eﬃciently than we know how to do classically.
